catalog_citation: Kelkar, Ashok R. 1968. Studies in Hindi-Urdu I: Introduction and Word Phonology. (Building Centenary and Silver Jubilee Series 35.) Poona: Deccan College Postgraduate and Research Institute.
catalog_quote: The procedure for predicting the tonic (and the subtonic, if any) in a word is as follows : Having marked the vowels as short (ɪ ʊ ə) and long (i e u o a) and having marked the phonologic syllable cuts (as described above), grade these syllables in the following ascending order of heaviness— Light : a syllable ending in a short vowel; Medium : a syllable ending in a long vowel or having a short vowel checked by a single nonsyllabic; Heavy : any other syllable. (Please note that /ⁿ/ is being ignored here.) Find the maximally heavy syllable or syllables. If there is only one maximum, it is tonic; the remaining preceding and following syllables, if any, are alternately atonic and subtonic, those adjacent to the tonic being atonic. If there are more than one maximum, the last but one out of the maxima is the tonic; the heavy syllable(s) preceding the tonic, if there are any, are all subtoni…
sweep_summary: Six title hits for Hindi. Three were read in full (Dyrud 2001 MA thesis already held by the project; Jyothi et al. 2014 and Genzel & Kügler 2010 downloaded from the ISCA archive and with and updated). Dyrud is the only item whose topic is Hindi word stress: it restates Hussain's (1997) weight rule (last heavy syllable stressed, penult if all light, final mora extrametrical) and concludes from production/perception data that Hindi-Urdu is non-stress-accent, which refines but does not contradict the catalog's weight-hedged coding on Kelkar 1968. Genzel & Kügler give a one-line secondary confirmation (weight-driven, ultima extrametrical) plus a first-hand stress-position table for 37 adjectives; Jyothi et al. is a prominence-perception study silent on placement. Three items stay unread behind paywalls: Sisson 1971 (De Gruyter; medium priority, a dedicated 26-page Hindi stress description), the Lahiri & Kennard 'Indian Subcontinent' chapter of the Oxford Handbook of Language Prosody (OUP; medium), and Féry, Pandey & Kentner 2016 (Benjamins; abstract read, focus prosody, low). No open repository copy of any of the three exists per OpenAlex, Unpaywall, Crossref, archive.org, and HathiTrust checks; Nothing read supersedes Kelkar 1968 as the deciding source.

new_statements.quote: Generally, the location of word stress in Hindi-Urdu is predictable on the basis of syllable weight. [...] Hindi-Urdu syllables can be classified as monomoraic or 'light' (V), bimoraic or 'heavy' (VV or VC), or trimoraic or 'superheavy' (VVC or VCC). Given these definitions, Hussain (1997) explains that the last heavy syllable is stressed, and if all syllables are light, the penultimate syllable is stressed. This account assumes a notion of extrametricality, which says the final mora of the word is invisible to the stress rule.
new_statements.citation: Dyrud, Lars O. 2001. Hindi-Urdu: stress accent or non-stress accent? MA thesis, University of North Dakota.
new_statements.locator: §1.2.3 Hindi-Urdu Stress, p. 4 (text extraction lines 323-331); conclusion p. vi and p. 28
new_statements.reading: weight-sensitive, unbounded-to-the-right placement: stress the last heavy (or superheavy) syllable with the word-final mora invisible, penult when every syllable is light. Dyrud's own experiments add that the acoustic marks of this stress (low pitch plus lengthening) surface only under focus, so he classes Hindi-Urdu as non-stress-accent. This is a summary of Hussain 1997 rather than Dyrud's own description, and it uses a two-way weight scale where Kelkar 1968 uses three grades with a 'last but one of the maxima' tie rule; both agree on weight sensitivity, so it supports the catalog's weight-hedged coding without replacing it.

sources.citation: Jyothi, Preethi, Jennifer Cole, Mark Hasegawa-Johnson & Vandana Puri. 2014. An investigation of prosody in Hindi narrative speech. Proc. Speech Prosody 7, 623-627.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Many early works studied the phenomenon of lexical stress in Hindi words which manifests itself as prominence via a designated syllable [1, 2, 3, 4] and acoustic evidence for lexical stress in Hindi [1, 2, 4, 5]. [...] Most recently, Féry and colleagues [6, 9, 11] claim that Hindi does not have prominence-lending pitch accents and uses only prosodic phrasing to structure an utterance, with edge-marking phrase tones. As evidence for this claim, they note that Hindi speakers do not produce a consistent pattern of pitch movement on a stressed syllable, and in general have very weak intuitions about the location of stress prominence at the word level.
sources.note: Perception study (10 naive listeners vs one expert) of prominence and phrase boundaries in narrative Hindi plus AuToBI automatic labeling; no statement of where word stress falls. Background only: notes early work on lexical stress and Féry's claim that speakers have weak intuitions about stress location. Finding: listeners agree far less on prominence (mean kappa 0.167) than on boundaries (0.582).
